paragraphs: […] In their account: those scribes who altered these eighteen passages were Ezra the scribe and Nehemiah. Tell us, then: why did they do this? What impelled them? Their answer must be: when the plain reading of these passages seemed to one who heard it ugly and unseemly, they wished to exalt God and exalt His Book above any expression that would offend the hearer and provoke him to fault-find against it. So they altered the passages for that reason. There are then two charges against this position. First: he who altered and substituted was wiser and more knowledgeable than the prophets who originally inscribed them. This is corruption in the extreme — that Ezra and Nehemiah should be more wise than Moses (peace upon him) — and indeed the corruption extends to God Himself, who originally spoke the words "and the Lord stood yet before Abraham" (with all its alleged ugliness). So he who altered it was wiser than God — and this alone is kufr from anyone who proposes it.[{2}] Second: he who wrote in place of the original — if his motive was preserving God's dignity, he should have concealed the alteration entirely, not publicly hung the original on the alteration, calling out "this used to be such-and-such." By his very act of altering and announcing the alteration, he has changed the Book without gaining anything, since the ugly original remains in place by the very announcement, and the unseemliness is not removed. And especially given their position that the present Torah is itself Ezra's compilation — if Ezra alone worked on it, what compelled him to say "this used to be thus, and I changed it"? Why didn't he just write it as he wanted? Is there a more contemptible or self-defeating position than this?

Now to the cases one by one. Case 1 (Gen 18:22): "and Abraham stood yet before the Lord." The narrative does not support their claim; rather, it supports the current text. Scripture begins (v. 1): "and the Lord appeared to him." Then (v. 2): "and he lifted up his eyes and looked." Then (v. 3): "and he said, with eagerness: My Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, pass not, I pray, from your servant." His statement "the Lord appeared" — its explication is "and he lifted up his eyes and looked." When God reveals Himself it is by manifesting one or another of these things: sending an angel or angels; lights He causes to shine; a miracle He sets up; or the like. And "pass not" is addressed to the angels — Abraham asked them not to depart until he had performed the hospitality detailed below. The evidence: (i) the request "pass not" is immediately after "ran to meet them" (v. 2) — and if the Lord had been in attendance with no angel intervening, Abraham's request not to pass would have preceded running-and-greeting; (ii) immediately after "pass not" he says (v. 4), "I shall fetch a morsel of bread for you" — a plural addressee — so the two statements ("pass not" and "I shall fetch bread for you") form a single addressed unit, with no break.

If someone objects: "pass not from your servant" is addressed to one (singular), and "I shall fetch a morsel of bread for you" to multiple (plural); on the present reading there should have been plural throughout. We reply: the answer is plain. Scripture often addresses a group in the singular — that is one way. And it is also possible that "pass not" was directed primarily at the prominent one among the visitors (who was leading them), and then Abraham extended the speech to include all of them with the plural form. Then he reports the bringing of food and their eating and their asking him about Sarah (v. 9), and one of them gives the annunciation (v. 10) — proving the questioning was from the group but the announcement from one. Which corroborates our reading.

The next pericope (v. 17 onward): "and the Lord said: shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?" — citing the principle of Amos 3:7, "surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret to his servants the prophets." Then God reveals (v. 20), "the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great." The proof that this conversation took place with Abraham present standing before God is v. 23: "and Abraham drew near and said: wilt thou indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" — Abraham could not have said this unless the prior communication had reached him: he is responding to v. 20. So Abraham was standing before the Lord, hearing the revelation about Sodom. And v. 22 — "those turned thence toward Sodom and Abraham stood yet before the Lord" — means: those (the angels) went into Sodom; Abraham, however, remained standing before the Lord until the entire revelation was complete.

[Moses] said: "If you are imposing this on me as a punishment — then make my killing [the form of it]" — i.e., let them kill me (the murmurers), rather than I see them suffer. Moses had reason to fear the Israelites' violence (Exod 17:4, "What shall I do to this people? They are nearly ready to stone me"). At this moment too — at the demand for meat — he could not be assured of their goodwill, hence Num 11:13, "Whence shall I have flesh to give unto all this people?" — followed by 11:15: "if thus thou wilt deal with me, kill me, I pray thee." In other words: if you make me bear this, then let them kill me; I would rather they kill me than that I see their distress. (This refutes the alleged emendation "kill me" was "thy killing.")

Their reading "let her not be as one stillborn from our mother" is wrong on two grounds. (i) The verse is about Miriam's leprosy; the speaker (Moses) addresses Aaron about Miriam. The pronoun "her" is correct: the verse means, "let her (Miriam) not be as one stillborn, half of his flesh eaten away when he comes from his mother's womb." (ii) Their suggestion that "his mother" should be "our mother" because Aaron is Moses' brother is interpretive, but it does not require the change. The text reads "her … his mother's womb" intelligibly: Moses is making an analogy between Miriam's case and the case of one dead-born. The "his flesh" reading was supposedly "our flesh" — on the rationale (Gen 37:27) "he is our brother, our flesh." The interpretive significance: Moses is saying, "when your sister (who is from your seed) is afflicted and you do not intercede for her — it is as if part of you is gone, since the brother is the flesh of his brother's flesh." This reads the received text richly without requiring an emendation.

Their reading "thy eyes" was supposedly the original. But the plain Hebrew grammar of v. 14 is clear: ha-anashim ha-hem is third-person plural — "those men." The reproach is from Israel (Dathan, Abiram) against Moses, who is the man of the address; the anashim are others — i.e., the men of the wilderness, or the leaders. No emendation needed.

The Hebrew qillu lahem benav. Their reading: qillu lī benav, "his sons brought contempt upon Me." Q's reply: this is standard biblical usage — a piety-displacement euphemism in which the people's actions are described as "bringing contempt upon themselves" when in fact what is meant is "bringing contempt upon God." Cf. Ps 80:7, "they mock us"; Ps 44:11, "and they that hate us spoil for themselves"; Jer 42:20, "thou hast deceived [yourselves]." The form is the same. So one can read the received text as-is; no emendation needed.[{3}] A consistency challenge: if these emendators were so vigilant, why did they not also alter Mal 1:6 ("ye priests that despise My name") and Ps 94:7 ("they say: the Lord shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard")?

The "His eye" reading they propose for ʿonyī. Q's reply: are we to suppose that all the references in Scripture to "the eyes of the Lord" and "the ears of the Lord" were also altered, together with references to His "limbs"? He who altered this — let us suppose he then failed to alter all the rest?[{4}] God forbid. The plain meaning of the verse is satisfied: "perhaps the Lord will look on my affliction" — i.e., on the tears of my eyes during weeping; or, per Targum Yonatan, "perhaps He will have mercy on my tear."

The "to your gods" reading is alleged. But nothing in the narrative requires this. And if the goal was to spare Israel from blame, why did the alleged emendators not also alter Jer 2:28 ("for according to the number of thy cities are thy gods, O Judah")? Or Isa 5:12 ("they sought the Lord and said: He is not")?

For Ezek 8:17 ("the branch to their nose"), the same answer as for 1 Sam 3:13 holds: standard piety-displacement. For Hab 1:12 ("we shall not die"), the proposed emendation "you shall not die" — Q replies: God forbid. To claim that the prophet predicated death of God and the scribes then altered it — this is beneath a beast, let alone a human. The verse means: God exists eternally; the prophet was reflecting on the enemy (Nebuchadnezzar) whom God set up as a corrective discipline, and turned to God saying, "Are You not from eternity? My God, my Holy One — be with us, lest we die at the hand of this disciplinary enemy You have established." So the received text is right.

Mal 1:13: "ye snuffed at it" — at the commandment, not at God. Zech 2:12: "the apple of his eye" — the eye of him who would harm the touched one, not God's eye. Jer 2:11 ("my people has exchanged its glory"), Hos 4:7 ("they exchanged their glory for shame"), Ps 106:20 ("they exchanged their glory") — all referring to the people's glory before God being lost when they rebel, not God's glory.

Job 7:20 ("I am become a burden to myself"): explicated by Job 7:19, "nor leave me alone till I swallow my spittle" — i.e., "You have exposed me to suffering until I am a burden to myself." Cf. Isa 43:24 ("thou hast made me to serve with thy sins"); 1:14 ("ye are a burden to me"). Job 32:3 ("they condemned Job"): the verse reports Elihu's anger at Job's three friends, who had unjustly indicted Job. To suggest "they condemned God" is incoherent: the friends were defending God by indicting Job. No emendation needed. Lam 3:20 ("my soul … humbled in me"): the prophet's complaint about his own weakness during the catastrophe. The parallel Ezek 16:63 ("thou shalt remember and be ashamed and never open thy mouth again") establishes the form.

In treating these eighteen passages they alleged were altered, we have shown what stops any one of them from grounding their claim. Even if we had not discussed them, the general argument (Bab 18 §7 above) would have been enough. But the explication closes the door entirely. ---
